articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: US Coast Guard recruits largest class in nearly 40 years, beats goals for third straight year
articles.summary: The Coast Guard enlisted 5,445 active-duty members in fiscal year 2026, its largest class in nearly four decades as Force Design aims to add 15,000.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The U.S. Coast Guard recruited its largest enlisted class in nearly four decades during fiscal year 2026, surpassing its recruiting goals for the third consecutive year as the service works to expand its ranks. According to the Coast Guard, 5,445 active-duty members enlisted in fiscal year 2026, up from 5,204 in 2025 and 4,422 in 2024. The service also commissioned 346 active-duty officers, the second-highest total in its history. "These record-breaking recruitment numbers prove that the call to serve still resonates deeply across our country," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT "I am incredibly proud to stand beside these new Coast Guard men and women who have stepped up to defend our homeland," he continued. "They represent the very best of who we are, and we are going to make sure they have the tools, the training and the support to get the job done." During fiscal year 2026, the Coast Guard expanded its recruiting efforts, opening four recruiting offices in Miami, Florida; Long Island, New York; Austin, Texas; and the Netherlands. Coast Guard Vice Commandant Adm. Tom Allan said the numbers reflect growing interest in serving. COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN "We surpassed our recruiting goals because Americans are ready and willing to serve in the U.S. Coast Guard, conducting exciting missions that deliver results our Nation needs," Allan said. "This momentum is about more than numbers; it is about being the world’s best Coast Guard and building the workforce America needs," he added. "We are proud to welcome our newest members and grateful to our recruiters for continuing to deliver exceptional results." The service is also investing in new infrastructure to help train its expanding workforce. The Coast Guard awarded a $400 million contract to modernize Training Center Cape May in New Jersey, marking the largest shore construction award in the service's history. TRUMP TURNS TO EMERGING TECH GIANT IN MULTI-BILLION BID TO RAMP UP US SUBMARINE PRODUCTION The facility serves as the Coast Guard's sole basic training center for enlisted recruits, and the improvements are intended to accommodate its growing workforce. The recruitment gains come as the Coast Guard pursues a modernization initiative known as Force Design. articles.title: Yemeni government forces claim 1,860 Houthis ‘neutralised’
articles.summary: Yemeni government forces said in a social media post that they carried out 2,103 ‘precise targeting operations’.
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces said they have “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters since launching a large-scale counter-offensive to retake territory under control of the rebel group.

The spokesperson for the internationally recognised government’s army said in a social media post early on Thursday local time that they carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions across several fronts as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” operation.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced on Sunday the “Dawn of Yemen” operation to retake all Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014.

Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.

Forces aligned with the Yemeni government launched an operation on Tuesday to capture strategic territory near the strait and around the city of Mocha, which the Houthis had captured in September.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib.

The spokesperson for the coalition said in a statement the targets included ballistic missile sites including “11 mountain-based ballistic missile storages in Saada, command and control centres, communication systems, missile and weapons storages”.

The new operation followed Houthi attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport, according to the spokesperson.

Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said the attacks on the two airports killed three people.

One person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Kemi's family home pledge' and 'Badenoch invokes core Tory values'
articles.summary: Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch's speech at the Tory conference dominates Thursday's papers.
articles.body:
Most of the front pages lead with Kemi Badenoch's Conservative conference speech yesterday. "We're ready for the fight" " is the Daily Telegraph's verdict on the Tory leader's message. The Financial Times says her promises to cut taxes represent a return to core Conservative values, but the Guardian describes them as "prioritising the wealthiest" . The Daily Express believes Badenoch is a "no nonsense" leader - a phrase used by several papers - and that she heads a party that will stop what it describes as inheritance tax "raids". The Times says the Conservatives are now focused on wooing "Middle England".

"Reform not dodgy, says Reform" is the Daily Mirror's review of the party's internal investigation finding it did not breach electoral law, when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing foreign donations. The paper describes the probe as a "white wash".

The i reports that a major government review will call for schoolchildren to be given help for ADHD, autism and mental health issues even before they are diagnosed. The paper says the report will also question whether the conditions are being over-diagnosed and recommend community-based support.

The Guardian warns that the government's reforms to the special education system in England could "unravel" because parents are rushing to secure support before any changes are implemented. It says experts are now urging ministers to review the timeline for their plans, which they claim are based on optimistic assumptions. The Department for Education says it's committed to implementing its plans by 2030.

A new daily pill could represent the biggest Parkinson's breakthrough since the 1960s, according to the Times. It says a clinical trial of Solengepras found it reduced patients' stiffness, slowness and tremors, as well as keeping them more alert.

The Telegraph says scientists could have found a key to helping us live longer in a 194-year-old giant tortoise called Jonathan. He lives on the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic and is estimated to have hatched in 1832. Researchers say he has the "super genes" of a 5-year-old that reduce inflammation, regulate insulin and suppress cancer.

articles.title: 'Developed cracks after quake': 21-year-old pregnant woman, 2 kids dead as building collapses in Delhi's Seemapuri
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Three people, including two children, died as a five-storey building collapsed in Seemapuri in northeast Delhi.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three people, including two children, died as a five-storey building collapsed in Seemapuri in northeast Delhi.This comes a month after a paying guest facility housing Delhi University students collapsed in south Delhi’s Satya Niketan, killing seven people.Those killed in Wednesday’s collapse included a 12-year-old unidentified girl; Gulafsha, a 21-year-old woman who was around four months pregnant; and a young child whose age has not been ascertained yet. An officer said the girl’s body was recovered from the debris, with her head severed. Eight others were pulled out from the rubble with injuries.Building developed cracks after quake a day earlier: ResidentsThe injured persons have been identified as Momin Mirja (56), Abdaan (3), Abdul Rehman (28), Devruddin (28), Salma (50), Chote (34), Sakina (35) and Samad (30). While some of them were inside the building when the structure collapsed, others were sitting on the roadside.The building, located in E-Block near Idgah Machhli Mandi, collapsed around 3.10-3.15pm in a densely populated slum area. Delhi Fire Service received the call around 3.30pm and rushed fire tenders and rescue teams to the spot. Delhi Police, MCD and Delhi Disaster Management Authority teams also joined the operation, while an NDRF team reached the site later.In a post on X Wednesday night, CM’s office said rescue and relief operations were underway at the site. “Every effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped under the debris and provide prompt medical care to the injured. Chief minister Rekha Gupta has directed all agencies concerned and officers to maintain close coordination, expedite rescue efforts and ensure all necessary assistance and care for those affected. The situation is being continuously monitored,” it stated.MCD said the structure stood on a plot belonging to Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board (DUSIB), measuring about 25 square yards, and was 20-25 years old. Officials described it as a ground-plus-three-storey building, while local residents said it had five storeys.The collapse damaged two adjoining buildings, with portions of the walls of one structure also coming down. The boundary wall of a nearby idgah was damaged as well.Local residents told MCD officials that several ragpicker families lived in the vicinity and were collecting plastic and other recyclable material when the building collapsed. They also said the building had developed cracks following the earthquake reported in the area a day earlier. They claimed the owner had subsequently been trying to vacate the structure. Police have not verified these claims.Rescue teams used heavy machinery to clear the rubble and search for survivors. Four JCB machines and several ambulances were deployed at the site. Sniffer dogs were also called in to aid the rescue operation. Power supply to the area was cut after the collapse damaged an electricity pole and snapped wires leading towards the nearby market.Rescuers faced difficulties because of the narrow lanes and densely populated surroundings. articles.title: California woman accused of spying for China will be jailed while awaiting trial
articles.summary: Wanying Zhang, a California woman accused of acting as a Chinese spy inside the U.S., will remain jailed pending her trial after a judge sided Wednesday with federal prosecutors who argued that she poses a flight risk.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — A California woman accused of acting as a Chinese spy inside the U.S. will remain jailed pending her trial after a judge sided Wednesday with federal prosecutors who argued that she poses a flight risk. Wanying Zhang, 34, who sometimes goes by Heather, will remain in pretrial detention following the ruling by U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim. The FBI arrested her Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she could board a flight to China. In a criminal complaint, prosecutors accused Zhang of spying on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his residence in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. Zhang, of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of downtown Los Angeles, hadn’t registered as a foreign agent as required, they said. Zhang was represented in court Wednesday by veteran criminal defense attorney Craig Harbaugh, who argued she wouldn’t flee in part because of her strong family connections to Southern California, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters. “The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said. Zhang’s family had been willing to put up their home equity — valued at $700,000 — combined with bonds from her husband, his sister, his father and a family friend totaling $120,000 as an assurance that she would appear in court. But prosecutors countered that she had “hundreds of thousands of dollars available to her” in China, as well as investments in a business and contacts that could allow her to flee easily. “I don’t think it’s a very strong argument that she’s that tied to her family here,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Elbogen said, casting Zhang as a lying foreign agent with the skills and resources to evade detection and capture. An investigation found Zhang attended China’s University of International Relations, which an FBI investigator said in court documents is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus.” The charging document alleges Zhang had been communicating with a former classmate, who is now believed to be a Chinese official, through whom she had arranged an agreement to conduct surveillance of the Taiwanese president’s son. The document says she later captured photos, video and license plate information about him and sent them to her alleged Chinese handler. She is alleged to have done all of that alongside an unidentified “Individual 1,” according to the complaint, who prosecutors said Wednesday had already fled to China two weeks ago. Zhang wore a white jail jumpsuit and remained shackled for the entirety of Wednesday’s proceedings, a departure from her initial appearance Monday, when she was uncuffed and wore street clothes, with her hair neatly styled. Wednesday’s hearing had several testy moments among prosecutors, Harbaugh and Kim, largely over whether Zhang’s pattern of one-way flights overseas was a credible defense that she wasn’t a flight risk and whether she had other U.S. properties to rely on for monetary assets. Discussion in court revealed Zhang had disclosed only one residence to pretrial services, while her husband later revealed they owned two more, which her attorney said was a misunderstanding. “She lied to pretrial services. She’s a real estate agent; she should know what properties she owns,” Elbogen countered. Zhang is due back in court as early as Oct. 19 for a preliminary hearing — if federal prosecutors don’t indict her before then.

articles.title: Texas carries out first execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injection
articles.summary: Lawyers for Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution after Christa Pike's botched lethal injections.
articles.body:
A death row inmate was executed by lethal injection on Wednesday evening in Texas, the first execution in the US since the failed attempt to put Christa Pike to death last week.

Lawyers for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution in light of Pike's botched injections last week, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.

But courts denied their requests, and he received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was pronounced dead at 20:03 local time.

Howard was convicted and sentenced to death for the 2000 murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery he committed.

His lawyers had argued that because Texas planned to inject Howard with the same drug - pentobarbital - that was used on Pike, he faced the same risks. They also alleged that Texas' supply of the drug had become degraded, as Pike's lawyers have similarly argued.

A court twice denied their appeals and the US Supreme Court also turned down the appeal late Wednesday.

"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys had argued, CBS reported.

Howard's attorneys also asked Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, to delay the execution by 30 days so they could seek additional information about the drug used in the execution. The governor did not grant the delay.

Howard was 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, who was working at a convenience store in Texas. Howard stole a carton of cigarettes and $114 from the register.

Asked if he had a final statement before his execution, Howard apologized to Swartout's family, who watched from a witness room, US media report.

"I wish that you accept my apology, and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

articles.title: Cornell defendant is fighting AG Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor
articles.summary: A petition filed Wednesday for Gillio Lopes says James has “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants.”
articles.body: One of the seven men named in the lawsuit filed by a former Cornell University student who alleges that she was sexually assaulted at an on-campus fraternity house has filed a petition to block New York Attorney General Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor in the case. The attorney for Gillio Lopes, who has denied that he sexually assaulted the woman, filed a petition in Albany County Supreme Court on Wednesday. His filing says James should not be the prosecutor in the case because she has “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants named in the Civil Case.” The Article 78 petition, filed against James and Gov. Kathy Hochul, is a proceeding used to challenge an action by a state or local government officer or agencies in New York. Hochul appointed James last week to independently investigate Jane Doe’s allegations in the lawsuit, in which she says she was plied with alcohol, sexually assaulted and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. In her role, James will determine whether criminal charges are warranted. James’ office declined to comment on the Article 78 filing. In a statement Monday, James said: “My office enforces our state’s laws to protect all New Yorkers. I am committed to leading a comprehensive investigation they can trust, guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.” Hochul’s office reiterated support for James on Wednesday. Reached for comment on Lopes’ filing, the governor’s office referred to her comments last week. “I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case,” Hochul said at the time. Hochul appointed James after she expressed dismay over Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s investigation of Doe’s allegations. He has said his office found a lack of criminality at the time and declined to press charges, but he reopened the case after the lawsuit sparked national uproar. Jane Doe’s civil suit was filed last month against Cornell, Chi Phi and seven fraternity brothers. None of the men named have been criminally charged. The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred. Cornell said in a statement Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation in 2024 that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions” from the university. Two of the fraternity members were expelled, and two others were suspended. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and required to write “reflection papers,” according to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation. Lopes’ filing argues that James’ appointment is “improper” and cites a post her office shared on X on Sept. 28, three days before her appointment was announced. In the post, she said: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.” The post, the petition contends, “made clear that she has formed an opinion about the case” and that “she has already reached the conclusion that Petitioner and the other named Defendants are guilty.” The petition also seeks to have the court review James’ appointment and asks that her appointment be annulled or modified so she is not personally directing the probe or any resulting prosecution. Stuart Bernstein, an attorney for Lopes, said Wednesday: “As Governor Hochul has said, the public needs confidence in the individual leading this investigation. AG James, based upon her very public statements validating Jane Doe, certainly doesn’t instill confidence in a fair investigation.” In her lawsuit, Doe accuses Lopes of kissing her and sexually assaulting her without her consent. Attorneys for two of the seven men, including Lopes, have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the other men. On Tuesday, Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney for Lopes, said he welcomes Cornell’s decision to have an independent review of its handling of Doe’s allegations, which will be led by former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates. “In our experience, Cornell’s investigations have generally been thorough. That said, we have also seen due process problems that have affected respondents, and on at least two occasions we have gone to federal court to try to address those issues. In this case, we do not agree with the outcome as to Mr. Lopes,” Miltenberg said.

articles.title: Okinawa governor wants discipline for U.S. military in Japan after murder is linked to Marine
articles.summary: The U.S. military had earlier restricted troops from leaving their base on the southern island following the Marine’s arrest on accusations that he robbed and killed a local woman.
articles.body: TOKYO — The governor of Okinawa demanded Wednesday that Japan’s central government do more to ensure effective discipline among U.S. service members on the southern island following the arrest of a U.S. Marine on accusations that he robbed and killed a local woman. Gov. Genta Koja, in Tokyo for the first time since taking office a week ago, conveyed Okinawa’s outrage in his meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, asking her government for further efforts to reduce the burden of hosting U.S. military bases on the small island. “Okinawa has requested preventive measures every time similar crimes were repeated in past, and now we have this case again,” Koja told Takaichi in a guest room at the Prime Minister’s Office packed with reporters. “I must say past disciplinary measures and human rights education implemented by the U.S. military have not worked at all,” Koja said. People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy U.S. military presence on the island and complained about noise, pollution and crime related to American bases, though some have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China. Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old Ohio native belonging to the Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested over the weekend on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media. Takaichi said she regretted the “heinous crime” and shared the outrage. Noting the new disciplinary measures announced by the U.S. military Tuesday, Takaichi said she expected the American government to take subsequent steps. Japan and the U.S. will discuss “how to implement preventive measures that are effective,” she said. Hours earlier, the U.S. military in Okinawa announced a 48-hour pause of all military operations for training through noon on Friday, as well as restricting the ability of troops to leave their base and prohibiting consumption of alcohol. Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, wrote in a letter posted Tuesday on X that episodes like these “demand we pause for reflection” and that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.” U.S. troops on Okinawa will be under a curfew from midnight to 5 a.m. for 30 days following the two-day training period, Watson said. Koja said he appreciated the prompt response from the Japanese and U.S. governments to the murder case “as a sign they both took the case seriously.” However, he will need to see details of the ongoing training, he said, and requested Japanese involvement to make U.S. disciplinary measures more effective. A majority of the more than 50,000 U.S. troops stationed in Japan under a bilateral security agreement are based on the island. Earlier Monday, Koja made the same request in his meeting with Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.

articles.title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
articles.summary: Students' blockades and marches spring from real grievances – and from France's habit of settling policy on the street.
articles.body:
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.

The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.

The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.

"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.

There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 7 pm, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.

France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.

The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.

Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?

According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.

Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.

Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.

The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.

In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.

And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.

Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.

To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.

In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.

In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.

On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.

Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.

The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.

French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.

The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.

In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.

On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BMFTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.

Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.

The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.

His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.

But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.

Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

articles.title: Nana Patekar: Bollywood actor dies at 75 in Goa home
articles.summary: Known for his intense performances, Patekar carved out a distinctive place in Indian cinema.
articles.body:
Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense performances and distinct dialogue delivery, has died at the age of 75 in Goa, his son Malhar told BBC Marathi.

One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing complex, often volatile characters. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.

He was rushed to hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday.

"Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency.

On Thursday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi led tributes to the actor, praising Patekar's versatility and outspoken personality.

Patekar portrayed characters that would "remain etched in the memory of generations", Modi wrote on X, adding that his death had left "a vast void in the artistic world".

Bollywood star Akshay Kumar, who appeared alongside Patekar in the comedy film Welcome, remembered him as a rare performer whose voice, intensity and honesty could command an audience's attention.

Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. His portrayal of the volatile, gritty gangster Anna won him his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award.

He didn't look back after this and played many memorable characters in several films through the 1990s. The range of the characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery over his craft.

His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. Then there was the villainous character of Majid Khan in Angaar, the patriotic firebrand of Tirangaa, and, most notably, Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, for which he won the national award for best actor.

Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.

Director Prakash Jha's Rajneeti in 2010 added another dimension to his acting as his portrayal of an astute politician was delivered with perfection.

The breadth of Patekar's career showcases the wide range of his work. He has played gangsters, soldiers, policemen, politicians, patriots, villains, comic characters and tragic figures, while moving between Hindi and Marathi cinema and sometimes also working behind the camera as a director and writer.

His three national awards for Parinda, Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi are a testament to his career.

Patekar was also an influential figure in both Marathi and Hindi theatre. Before cinema made him a familiar face, he spent years working in theatre, where he developed his gritty style of dialogue delivery and also mastered the intensity he brought to his on-screen characters.

Purush and Hamidabai Chi Kothi were two of his most famous plays. Despite being successful in films, he remained active in theatre throughout his professional life.

Patekar was also known for his activism and didn't mince his words while criticising the government of the day. He was direct, and almost brazen and unapologetic, when it came to criticising ministers and their policies and that too quite publicly.

Issues related to farmers were particularly close to his heart.

His work moved beyond just giving statements. In 2015 he and actor Makarand Anaspure established the Naam Foundation, which has worked on farmer welfare and water conservation in Maharashtra.

But his career was not without controversies.

In 2018, allegations of sexual harassment made by actor Tanushree Dutta against Patekar over an alleged incident on a film set a decade earlier helped spark India's #MeToo movement . Patekar denied the allegations.

In 2019, he was cleared of the charges after police said they had not found sufficient evidence against him.

articles.title: Texas executes Jamaal Howard despite concerns over lethal injection drug used in failed Tennessee execution
articles.summary: Jamaal Howard's attorneys cited Christa Pike's failed lethal injection in Tennessee to argue the pentobarbital drug posed risks, but the Supreme Court rejected it.
articles.body: A Texas man convicted of killing a convenience store clerk during a robbery was executed Wednesday evening after the Supreme Court declined to halt the execution, despite his attorneys raising concerns about the lethal injection drug used in a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week. Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. He was sentenced to death for the 2000 killing of 42-year-old Vickie Swartout in Silsbee, Texas. Prior to Howard's execution, his attorneys pointed to the failed execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30, arguing that the same drug Texas planned to use could pose similar risks. "Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee’s footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys argued in their filing. CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS The Supreme Court rejected Howard's emergency appeal without explanation. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent, Fox News reported. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals had previously rejected two requests to stop the execution based on concerns about the drug's use. According to The Associated Press, as the pentobarbital began taking effect Wednesday evening, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped. Howard then began making snoring sounds, coughed and resumed the snoring sounds, which grew progressively quieter. His movements reportedly stopped entirely after around 30 seconds, and he was pronounced dead 19 minutes later. CHRISTA PIKE’S BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTION TAKES FOCUS OFF VICTIM, JEOPARDIZES EXECUTION: FORMER POLICE CHIEF Howard's attorneys also said in court filings that they had requested information about the dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use to carry out the execution. The concerns stemmed in part from Pike's execution attempt, during which she reportedly survived two doses of pentobarbital. Howard's execution took place the same day a Tennessee judge granted a request from Pike's attorneys to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence connected to the failed execution attempt. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the first person to survive a lethal injection in the modern era. CHRISTA PIKE EXECUTION FAILURE SPARES MURDERER WHO BAILED VICTIM OUT JUST TO KILL HIM Howard's attorneys also argued before the Supreme Court that his execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. However, the state said his attorneys had not presented evidence establishing that he met the legal criteria for intellectual disability. Howard, who was 20 years old at the time, also took $114 from the cash register during the robbery. Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Syria considers sending troops to Saudi Arabia to fight Houthis
articles.summary: Syria is considering sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help fight Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, Reuters reported, citing a US official and a Syrian
articles.body: Syria is considering sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help fight Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, Reuters reported, citing a US official and a Syrian military official familiar with the discussions.According to Reuters, Syria is looking at several options, from providing defensive support and expertise to help Saudi Arabia counter Houthi missile and drone attacks, to potentially sending Syrian troops to fight alongside Saudi-backed Yemeni forces.No final decision has been taken, and Damascus has not confirmed any plan to deploy combat troops.The US official told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had asked Syria to deploy forces to fight the Houthis. However, the Syrian government has not publicly confirmed that it has agreed to send troops to Yemen.A Syrian diplomat told Reuters that Damascus “stood firmly with Saudi Arabia” against Houthi attacks but stressed that Syria's priority remained its domestic recovery after years of war. The diplomat said any military cooperation or exchange of expertise with Saudi Arabia would take place “exclusively through official channels” and under existing bilateral agreements.The development comes as Saudi Arabia steps up its military campaign against the Houthis after the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi territory.Syria-Saudi relationsThe possible Syrian military support for Saudi Arabia comes as relations between Damascus and Riyadh have strengthened significantly since Ahmed al-Sharaa took power.Saudi Arabia has emerged as an important political and economic partner for Syria as the new government tries to rebuild the country after 14 years of civil war.In February, Syria and Saudi Arabia signed a multibillion-dollar investment package covering aviation, energy, real estate and telecommunications, underscoring Riyadh's role in Syria's economic recovery.Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on October 6. According to Syria's state news agency SANA, the two leaders discussed bilateral relations, regional developments and ways to expand cooperation between the two countries.The bigger pictureSince the fall of Bashar al-Assad, Damascus has largely tried to avoid getting pulled into regional wars while concentrating on rebuilding its institutions and integrating former rebel groups into a new Syrian army.Reuters reported that Syria had previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon for similar reasons.A decision to help Saudi Arabia against the Houthis would therefore represent a major shift. The Houthis are backed by Iran, while Saudi Arabia is now leading a renewed campaign against the group after weeks of missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.For Saudi Arabia, bringing Syria into the conflict could provide another Arab partner as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces attempt to push back the Houthis.For al-Sharaa, however, sending Syrian troops could expose his still-fragile military to a new conflict and risk worsening relations with Iran, Hezbollah and Iran-aligned Iraqi militias.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Proud of our air warriors': President Murmu, PM Modi hail IAF on Air Force Day
articles.summary: President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah on Thursday extended greetings to the country's air warriors,
articles.body: President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah on Thursday extended greetings to the country's air warriors, veterans and their families, while highlighting the Indian Air Force’s courage, professionalism and combat preparedness.The IAF marked its 94th Air Force Day, commemorating 94 years since the force was established on October 8, 1932.President Murmu said the IAF has rendered exemplary service to the nation and specifically praised its role in Operation Sindoor, saying the operation demonstrated the courage, precision and operational preparedness of Indian air warriors in safeguarding national security.“Operation Sindoor demonstrated the courage, precision and operational preparedness of our air warriors in safeguarding the nation’s security,” Murmu said.Prime Minister Modi said the country was proud of its air warriors and saluted their courage and commitment to protecting India’s skies.“India is proud of our Air Warriors. On Air Force Day, we salute their courage and commitment to protect our skies,” Modi said.Amit Shah described IAF personnel as “warriors of our skies”, praising their valour, precision and striking capabilities while paying tribute to those who laid down their lives for the nation.“A legion of real-life bravehearts whose saga of invincible valour, laser-sharp precision and devastating striking capabilities is testified by the Earth and satellites in faraway space,” Shah said.Evolution of the Indian Air ForceThe Indian Air Force has evolved from a small air arm established in 1932 into a modern aerospace force with capabilities spanning air superiority, precision strike, air defence, surveillance, strategic airlift and humanitarian operations.Established on October 8, 1932, as the Royal Indian Air Force, it began with a small fleet and limited operational capability. The force expanded considerably during World War II, gaining combat experience in the Burma theatre.After Independence in 1947, the IAF became a crucial part of India's defence architecture. It played a major role in the 1947-48 Kashmir conflict and subsequently underwent significant modernisation. The 1962 war with China and the 1965 India-Pakistan war highlighted the need to strengthen India's air power and develop greater self-reliance.Over the following decades, the IAF inducted platforms such as the MiG-21, MiG-23, MiG-27, Jaguar and Mirage 2000, while India also began developing indigenous aircraft, including the Tejas.During the 1999 Kargil conflict, the IAF conducted Operation Safed Sagar, with Mirage 2000 fighters carrying out precision strikes against Pakistani positions in difficult mountainous terrain. The operation demonstrated the growing importance of precision air power.In the 2000s and 2010s, the IAF further expanded its capabilities with platforms such as the Su-30MKI, upgraded Mirage 2000s, C-17 and C-130J transport aircraft and Apache attack helicopters.Today, the IAF operates a mix of Rafale, Su-30MKI, Tejas and other combat aircraft, supported by airborne early-warning systems, transport aircraft, helicopters, drones, air-defence systems and precision weapons.Its modernisation is increasingly focused on indigenous platforms, long-range precision strike, unmanned warfare, integrated air defence and network-centric operations.

articles.title: South Korea pledges legal action over alleged fuel exports to Russia
articles.summary: Ukrainian reports of South Korean fuel exports to Russia come amid strained tensions between Seoul and Kyiv.
articles.body:
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said the government will take legal action over illegal fuel shipments to Russia if allegations from an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are confirmed.

The Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it had not confirmed whether South Korean fuel, including diesel, had been exported to Russia.

It added that exports of some products, such as diesel and jet fuel for commercial purposes, were not included in a South Korean exports control list to Russia.

On Wednesday, the South Korean presidential office dismissed a statement by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on sanctions policy, that 176,000 tonnes of fuel were shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers in July and August.

Ukraine’s top sanctions official said the alleged findings run counter to South Korea’s sanctions policy towards Russia.

“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, our government has consistently implemented sanctions and export controls against Russia in close cooperation with the international community,” South Korean presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said on Wednesday, according to the Yonhap news agency.

“We ask that Ukraine also refrain from distorting the relevant policies of the Republic of Korea without sufficient verification of the facts and making public remarks that can damage international trust,” she added.

Relations between South Korea and Ukraine have been strained for the past couple of weeks after Seoul accused Zelenskyy of having “unilaterally disclosed” to the United Nations General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

Seoul Korea demanded an official apology from Kyiv, claiming the Ukrainian president had breached a non-disclosure agreement. Kyiv said no such agreement was in place.

Pyongyang and Moscow, meanwhile, have deep ties, with the two countries having signed a mutual defence treaty in 2024. According to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, about 14,000 to 15,000 North Korean soldiers were sent to support Russia’s war efforts against Ukraine.

North Korea and South Korea remain technically at war because the 1950–1953 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

articles.title: Funding to help people access healthy food and tackle child obesity
articles.summary: Local authorities in Hull and Lincolnshire have each been given £220,000.
articles.body:
People in Hull are facing a "stark" challenge when it comes to accessing healthy food, the leader of the city's council says.

The local authority and four from Lincolnshire are among 45 in England that will each receive £222,000 from the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) to help improve access to healthy and affordable food.

The authorities were chosen after being identified as having the greatest levels of deprivation and childhood obesity.

Councillor Mike Ross, leader of Hull City Council, said: "It can be incredibly difficult for some people to get the healthy food they need. So, anything that helps tackle those barriers is really important."

DEFRA said the Good Food Neighbourhoods funding could support schemes such as community food shops and mobile greengrocers, as well as helping local authorities strengthen their capacity to plan for and meet local food needs.

The National Child Measurement Programme for the school year 2024/25 shows 10.2% of children in reception year (aged 4-5) in Hull had a BMI status of obese, while in Year 6 (aged 10-11) that figure was 19%.

Those figures are above the national average .

Ross added: "This whole picture demonstrates there is severe need here.

"Of course, this funding will help tackle that, building on the work that's already taking place and wanting to work with not just the council but with local communities and groups across the city to make sure everything is done to support local residents."

Darren Squires, from the Hull Food Partnership, which brings together all the community food organisations in the city, said it was not just a case of low income that made it difficult for people to access food.

He said: "When we talk about deprivation, some of it is poverty, some of it is access to food if you're so far away from a supermarket and don't drive or if you're running two jobs.

"For some people it's not about income. People can be financially secure, but still time poor.

"There are areas in the city where it is much easier to get a takeaway meal than it is to get any other kind of food that you would cook at home."

Other local authorities from East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire allocated the funding include North East Lincolnshire Council (NELC), North Lincolnshire Council, City of Lincoln Council and South Holland District Council.

Councillor Nige Oliver, portfolio holder for health, wellbeing and adult social care at NELC, welcomed the announcement.

He said: "Families in areas like ours can face significant challenges in trying to access affordable, healthy food.

"We're now looking at how we can use this funding to support people in our area."

The BBC understands a government meeting next week will provide further details to local authorities about this funding.

articles.title: Lancashire mushrooms: Forager sees 'bumper' autumn season
articles.summary: The RHS says the hot, dry summer followed by autumn rain could lead to record sightings.
articles.body:
Have you spotted more mushrooms than usual on woodland walks or in your garden this autumn?

Lancashire forager Colin Unsworth said some species had appeared in "bumper" numbers, although others had been harder to find.

But Unsworth, who leads foraging trips across Lancashire, warned people not to eat wild mushrooms unless they were certain they had identified them correctly, as some poisonous species can closely resemble edible varieties.

Unsworth, who runs Forest Horizons in Adlington, said fly agaric, the distinctive red mushroom with white spots, and blushers had been found in good numbers.

Porcini mushrooms, also known as penny buns or ceps, had been "a bit thin on the ground", he said. He added there was an EU-wide shortage of the edible fungi, which are prized by chefs for their "lovely, robust flavour".

However, he warned that some poisonous species, including the brown roll-rim, can be mistaken for edible mushrooms.

"You get look-alike mushrooms," he said. "They can be really dangerous."

The RHS said prolonged hot weather and drought, followed by a wet autumn, could help some fungi flourish.

Its advice team recorded a 43% rise in inquiries about garden fungi following the 2025 drought, compared with the previous year.

Some species benefit from extra dead plant material left by drought, while others respond to stress in trees by producing more mushrooms.

Jassy Drakulic, RHS senior plant pathologist, said gardeners could notice a "remarkable variety of mushrooms and toadstools" appearing in lawns, borders and around trees this autumn.

She said fungi were mostly a sign of a healthy ecosystem, helping to break down organic matter and support plant health.

For Unsworth, autumn is the highlight of the foraging calendar.

He said understanding mushrooms helped "join the dots" between different parts of the landscape and explain why species were found in particular habitats.

A typical forage at this time of year could produce 20 or 30 edible types of mushroom, he said.

"In the autumn time, mushrooms take centre stage and they're so beautiful and they're so varied," he said.

articles.title: Berkshire property with 'extensive' tunnel network put on market
articles.summary: The Tilehurst property, that includes a hand-built underground railway, will be up for auction this month.
articles.body:
A hand-built underground railway and an "extensive" network of tunnels and underground rooms are among the features hidden for decades beneath a property going to auction this month.

The subterranean network below the site on Long Lane in Tilehurst, Berkshire, descends through four levels, reaching more than 15m (49ft) below ground.

It was created during two decades by the property's previous owner, the late Tony Deane, who was a civil engineer with a passion for tunnelling.

Richard Worrall, auctioneer and consultant at BTG Eddisons Property Auctions, said the site "represents a really unique opportunity for somebody to either develop it or to live there and enjoy it".

The site comprises garden land, a swimming pool and a workshop at the back of the garden.

Worrall said: "To say it's a workshop is doing it down a little bit, it's constructed better than 95% of houses, to be honest."

Planning consent was granted by West Berkshire Council in December 2024 for a 5,000 sq ft (464.5 sq m) five-bedroom, two-storey house to be built on the site of the swimming pool, while conversion of the workshop has consent for conversion to a three-bedroom house.

The site is accessed via a secure gated driveway and includes a 2,500 sq ft (232.2 sq m) workshop arranged over three floors, parking, gardens, a swimming pool and changing rooms.

The complex hidden beneath the workshop contains more than 1,300 sq ft (120.7 sq m) of underground space, including tunnels and storage rooms, as well as two secret doors, one formed by a 1.5-tonne sliding concrete wall.

"It was, I think, a marvellous piece of vision and passion and great British eccentricity really - he had the skill set to do it," said Worrall.

Construction of the tunnels took place during the 1980s and '90s, with Deane carrying out the work himself, assisted by his family.

But it wasn't the family's first subterranean project, with construction of underground changing rooms next to the property's swimming pool taking place in the 60s.

The entrance was hidden behind a 23ft (7m) high rocket, which remains in place.

Despite the scale of the project, its existence is understood to have remained largely unknown outside the family, including to neighbours in the surrounding residential area.

Speaking on the tunnel network, Worrall, who has been doing his job for more than four decades, said he has "never seen anything like that before".

The property will go to auction over two days on 28 October with a guide price of £300,000 - £325,000.

Worrall said: "I think by its very nature it is going to attract a lot of interest from people who have got an idea of what they might want to use the tunnelling network for.

"Whether they be preppers [survivalists], or people who've got sensitive material they want to keep below ground, it keeps a constant temperature down there and would make a fantastic wine cellar.

articles.title: 'Boy's evil knife attack could have killed my daughter but he walked free from court'
articles.summary: The 14-year-old girl could have died in the frenzied attack, her mother says.
articles.body:
The mother of a 14-year-old girl who was repeatedly stabbed in an "evil" attack by a boy says it is "disgraceful" that he was not jailed.

The boy, 14, from Wiltshire, had stalked the girl after she refused to date him before attacking her with a 6in knife in broad daylight at a shop in Cirencester, Gloucestershire, on 15 March.

Last month, he was sentenced to a three-year restraining order and a one-year referral order after he admitted wounding with intent, inflicting grievous bodily harm and possession of a bladed article in a public place.

The girl's mother said: "If it hadn't been for the shopkeeper and her [own] quick reactions, she would have been dead."

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it was currently "reviewing how the law can better protect victims in the youth courts" to ensure the "punishment fits the offence".

If you have been affected by issues of sexual abuse or violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

The 'little piece of post-war history hiding in plain sight'

City's only residential tower block to be demolished

The boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, waited for the victim to enter the shop as he watched her from a nearby car park.

He then followed her inside and stabbed her multiple times in a prolonged attack.

Det Supt Ian Fletcher said of CCTV of the attack: "Anyone who sees footage would say she is very lucky to not have very serious, if not fatal injuries."

He likened the attack to the award-winning TV drama Adolescence, in which a teenager fatally stabs his female classmate.

The mother added: "If you're big enough to commit an adult crime, you should have the punishment, regardless of your age. It was not a petty crime - it wasn't petty theft."

She told the BBC that the family remained "scared" after the boy's "evil and sick" attack.

She added that his age should not have spared him from a youth detention centre.

"I feel angry. We're incredibly let down; we feel like everyone's failed us," she said.

"It's disgusting. It's absolutely disgraceful after watching [footage of the attack] that someone can say the guidelines are 'first offence and the injuries weren't life-threatening'.

"They weren't life-threatening because she managed to defend herself.

"I want some justice for my child - I want some protection."

An MoJ spokesperson said they had received "multiple requests" to reconsider the sentence under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme, but sentences passed by youth courts are not part of the scheme.

"We share the public's shock at the details of this horrific crime," they added.

"Our thoughts are with the victim and her family, and we recognise it will be deeply disappointing that the sentence handed out cannot be referred to the court of appeal.

"We are reviewing how the law can better protect victims in the youth courts."

They added that sentencing decisions are made by independent judges and magistrates, in line with the sentencing guidelines.

Carole Gould, whose teenage daughter Ellie was murdered by her ex-boyfriend in May 2019, described the sentence as "wrong, immoral, and unjust".

Ellie was strangled and stabbed in the neck multiple times after she tried to end her three-month relationship with 17-year-old Thomas Griffiths.

After initially attempting to stage the scene as a suicide, Griffiths later admitted murder and was jailed for a minimum of 12 and a half years in November 2019.

"I'm absolutely appalled at the outcome of this case," she said.

"In my mind, there is no doubt about it - this was premeditated attempted murder.

"All I could think of was that poor girl and her family, and the terrible trauma that she's going to have to live with for the rest of her life."

Gould agreed "the outcome could so easily have been different", as many of the knife wounds were focused around the victim's neck.

"I thoroughly believe in rehabilitation, but equally, there has to be repercussions for such behaviour," she said.

"It just sends the message that violence against women and girls is not being taken seriously."

In a statement read out in court, the girl described having nightmares since the attack.

"I relive the incident, but in these dreams it happens in different places.

"I sleep in the dark but when I wake, I constantly feel like there is a presence in the room. I can't stop thinking about it," she said.

After the girl ended their brief relationship, she blocked the boy's number on her phone to prevent him from contacting her.

But The Hollie Gazzard Trust, a Gloucestershire charity that aims to raise awareness of and help reduce domestic violence, advised against this.

Jane Harvey, the charity's chief executive, warned obsessed partners are "more likely to physically come round and find you" when blocked.

She added: "If we have to go down the route of reporting to police and getting the criminal justice system involved, what we need is evidence of the unwanted contact in order for the police to be able to prosecute the case.

"By blocking someone, we potentially lose evidence that could help secure something like a conviction or a restraining order."

articles.title: Taunton Brewhouse closure leaves questions over ticket refunds
articles.summary: One ticketholder for a Taunton Brewhouse Theatre show says she has been able to contact the venue.
articles.body:
A ticketholder for a theatre performance cancelled when a venue announced its closure says she is disappointed not to have been offered a refund yet.

Susan Fone said despite calling and emailing the Brewhouse Theatre in Taunton, Somerset, she has been unable to get in touch with anyone regarding her tickets for a festive performance of Treasure Island.

Fone told BBC Your Voice that she was not informed of the theatre's closure over financial issues by the venue but instead found out in an online news article.

Taunton Theatre Association (TTA) has advised ticketholders to keep hold of their tickets for when the refunds process opens.

Chair of the TTA Val Hammond told the BBC that she was "very, very sorry to hear about the experience of ticket holders".

Hammond said the association was trying to upload all necessary guidance to its website and advised ticketholders to retain their proof of purchase as well as their tickets.

Taunton Brewhouse issued a statement on its website on 5 October announcing it would be closing at the end of this month due to financial pressures.

Hammond said that it was an "incredibly difficult moment for everyone connected to TTA".

"The theatre remains in the ownership of Somerset Council and we hope that, in due course, a new team of enthusiasts will bring the vision and the energy needed to reopen it," she added.

"I believe we are all united in thinking it inconceivable that Taunton should be without a public theatre."

In an interview with the BBC, Fone echoed this sentiment.

She said: "I'm very sad and extremely disappointed. I understand that funding for the arts is being withdrawn, but had these issues been publicised earlier, the community may have been able to raise the funds to keep it open.

"The theatre is extremely important to Taunton and we should do our utmost to retain what arts facilities we have in Somerset - they're limited anyway".

articles.title: How boxing inspired a play about men's mental health
articles.summary: The play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other.
articles.body:
For many athletes, years of training can provide a routine, a purpose and an identity - but what happens when it all stops?

That question is at the heart of a new play which explores men's mental health through the world of boxing.

The Corner Man follows a fighter forced to confront life outside the ring after spending years dedicated to the sport.

Through his story, the play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other.

Writer and producer Cathal J Ferris said the idea grew from his own experience of boxing and conversations with fighters.

"What is a boxer after he retires really played on my mind," he said, adding that the same questions around identity and purpose can apply beyond sport.

The play follows Liam Casey, who has dedicated much of his life to boxing, from the age of about nine into his 30s.

For Ferris, the story is not only about leaving the ring, but about losing the routine that comes with it.

"The idea of structure and what life is like whenever you lose that structure definitely played on my mind," he said.

"There are people who work in jobs for 10, 12, 13-odd years and just decide to change industries.

"I think there's a lot of people who may not know what to do with themselves after."

Ferris grew up performing in amateur theatre in Belfast and Lisburn before going to drama school in London in 2012.

He said returning home had given him the chance to tell new stories about the place where he grew up.

"I'm a Belfast boy at heart, and it is great to tell stories from the city," he said.

Ferris said "the boxing community in Belfast is phenomenal" and that it played an important part in shaping the story.

'If you're a man and you're struggling... speak to somebody'

Alongside boxing, the play also looks at how men talk - or sometimes do not talk - about their mental health.

"I think the old phrase is 'say nothing', and we know that all too well," Ferris said.

"As a man, it is definitely hard for myself to talk about these things, and I try to be a little bit more open."

In the play, Liam struggles with life after boxing, but it is the other men around him who help provide a support network - something Ferris said was an important part of the story.

"It is healthy to talk, so definitely if you're a man and you're struggling, at least speak to somebody," he said.

Director Emma Copeland said she knew relatively little about boxing before becoming involved in the production, but soon immersed herself in the sport.

"I got really into boxing and went to a load of boxing classes and still going," she said.

Copeland said she also watched films, read books and autobiographies and listened to podcasts to make sure she knew the world she was portraying.

For her, one of the most important parts of the play is the support the men offer each other.

"The angle that I see is that men supporting men, and helping and talking and encouraging support with each other and encouraging that conversation," she said.

"Rather than shutting it down or locking themselves away in their own feelings."

For actor Gary Trainor, the experience Liam goes through is not something that only applies to boxers.

Trainor, who plays gym owner Marty as well as several other roles, said suddenly losing something which has been central to your life could happen in many different circumstances.

"He's been so engrossed in the world of boxing for his entire life, to lose it in one injury and to try and figure out his life after that is, I think, probably universal in a lot of men's lives," he said.

"That could be maybe losing a job, anything like that."

Trainor described the play as "full of heart and humour" and said he hoped it would "make a few lads think".

For him, its message is a straightforward one - that "men should talk to each other a bit more about what they are feeling and how they are processing things".

articles.title: In 2013, buyers paid $3.45 million for a Lake Minnetonka property and built a 10,000-sq-ft home two years later; the estate has now sold for $18.25 million, setting a Minnesota record
articles.summary: A Lake Minnetonka estate in Deephaven has sold for $18.25 million, becoming Minnesota’s most expensive residential sale on record.
articles.body: A Lake Minnetonka estate in Deephaven has sold for $18.25 million, becoming Minnesota’s most expensive residential sale on record. The sale was reported by the Minnesota Star Tribune and Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal, while property records and the listing history independently confirm the October 1 closing. Located at 20670 Linwood Road, the lakefront property spans about 2.39 acres and includes 350 feet of shoreline. The contemporary residence measures 10,440 square feet, with five bedrooms, nine bathrooms and a heated six-car garage. It was designed by Charles Stinson and completed in 2015 by Streeter Custom Builder.The sale is notable not only for its price but also for the property’s transformation over the past 13 years. The land changed hands in 2013 for $3.45 million. At the time, the site carried an older 5,145-square-foot house dating to 1956. The existing custom-built residence was subsequently constructed on the property and completed in 2015.The estate had initially entered the market at $22 million in August 2025. It eventually sold for $18.25 million, representing a discount of roughly 17% from the original asking price. The closing took place on October 1, according to the property’s MLS history.Inside, the home is designed around expansive views of Lake Minnetonka. A large wall of sliding glass doors connects the main living areas with an outdoor terrace, screened porch and infinity pool. The property also includes a chef’s kitchen, separate support kitchen, two offices and glass-enclosed wine storage.The lower level adds another layer of luxury, with four junior suites, a bunk room, exercise room, wine cellar, billiards area, bar and recreation space. Outside, the estate has a private sandy beach and a separate lakeside boathouse equipped with a rooftop deck, kitchenette, half-bath, laundry facilities and outdoor shower.The landscaping was also extensively reworked after the property was acquired. Earlier reporting on the home said more than 240 mature trees were removed and more than 350 new trees were planted as part of the site’s redesign, helping create a more private setting around the modern residence.The $18.25 million transaction surpasses the previous Minnesota residential-sale record of $17.5 million, set by another Lake Minnetonka property in 2006. That record had remained in place for roughly two decades. The new record also highlights the strength of the luxury market around Lake Minnetonka. Recent high-value transactions include a $13.5 million Orono sale in 2023 and a $10 million Wayzata sale that same year. More recently, a Deephaven estate sold for $9.125 million, illustrating the growing number of multimillion-dollar transactions around the lake.Yet the $18.25 million property is not the most expensive Lake Minnetonka home currently being offered for sale. An estate in the Woodland area remains listed at $50 million, while another property was recently placed on the market for $26.5 million. Those are asking prices, however, rather than completed transactions, meaning the Linwood Road sale remains the benchmark for an actual residential closing.The buyer of the Deephaven estate has not been publicly identified. As the transaction settles into the public record, the sale stands as a striking example of how far the upper end of Minnesota’s residential market has moved since the property last changed hands for $3.45 million in 2013.

articles.title: Tree of the Year: Wonky wych elm in County Down wins title
articles.summary: It is the first time a tree in Northern Ireland has won the national title since it was launched in 2014.
articles.body:
Newcastle's 'Bendy Tree' has been crowned UK Tree of the Year 2026 - the first time a tree in Northern Ireland has won the national title since it was launched in 2014.

The 150-year-old wych elm on the central promenade took more than 30% of the national public vote.

The theme of the Woodland Trust's annual competition was Against All Odds, with trees across the UK shortlisted for being impressive, beautiful and sometimes baffling examples of how nature can survive adversity.

Northern Ireland director John Martin said he was rooting for the "whimsical" tree to win and said tens of thousands across the UK had clearly felt the same.

"It's a great testament to the resilience of nature."

The Bendy Tree in County Down saw off competition from a small yew that has been growing from the masonry of a Devon church tower for 200 years, a Scottish ash that survived a lightning strike, and a Surrey yew, in which early 19th Century villagers found an embedded English Civil War cannonball.

The wych elm is the last remaining tree of a row that was planted along the original promenade in the 19th century, to shelter it from the sea breeze.

The rest of the trees were felled in the 1980s during redevelopment.

The wind it protected people from has made its trunk grow almost horizontal.

But its leafy rainbow over the path means it is still protecting people - just slightly differently.

"The council have put a bench underneath it where people can come and sit in the shade and enjoy views of the Mournes and of the sea," Martin said.

"I think the whimsical nature of it and the fact that it's showed a lot of resilience over 150 years has proven it the winner this year."

But it has survived more than the weather.

As a native elm tree, it also resisted Dutch Elm disease, which destroyed most of the 30 million elms around the UK in the 1960s.

Martin said it had shown "remarkable resilience" to live as long as it has and added that it was "great" to see a tree of this age acknowledged.

The Ancient Tree inventory lead at the Woodland Trust, May Chemais, said it was an "astonishing and bizarre" tree that had endured a lot.

"The Bendy Tree has been blasted by extreme winds, over and over again, for well over a century.

"But it has continued to exist and remain rooted, adapting to its surroundings and flourishing into this unusual shape that is providing shade and joy to its community.

"We've all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are - I think that's why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people."

She added that older trees like the Bendy Tree are part of a community's culture, providing shade and stories.

Northern Ireland has one of the lowest rates of woodland cover in Europe (8.7%).

In UK terms, it lags behind Scotland (19%), Wales (15%), England (10%) and also the Republic of Ireland, which has 11% cover.

A tree-planting action plan has been launched, with a target of 12% woodland cover by 2050.

But tree-planting rates need to more than triple to get on track for that.
